title.narrative: Migration and Displacement Programme 2023-2028 - Independent Diplomat - "Nothing About Us Without Us: Strengthening Refugee Leadership in Diplomacy" (1 April 2024-31 March 2029))

description.narrative:
Independent Diplomat (ID) was selected as a Support Partner by the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs within the framework of its grant, Migration and Displacement 2023-2028. Through this funding support, ID began to implement the programme, “Nothing About Us Without Us: Supporting Refugee Leadership in Diplomacy” in April 2024. We developed our programme with full recognition of the challenges that refugees, the refugee-led organizations (RLOs) which represent them, and host communities experience in accessing the policy space at multiple levels. We seek to leverage our track record of advancing Meaningful Refugee Participation (MRP) at the global level to advance the meaningful participation of refugees and host communities in diplomatic processes in the countries that host the highest numbers of refugees, namely: Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Kenya, Türkiye, and Uganda.
The integrated objectives of our programme are threefold:
(I) Enable local organizations, in particular refugee-led organizations, networks and advocates to access the political space to make their voices heard and increase their operational impact to provide lasting and sustainable solutions for refugees and other displaced populations in regions of origin. (II) Strengthen refugee-led organizations’ expertise and capacity to independently influence political negotiations and build policy coherence from the international level to the local level. (III) Provide long-term core funding to RLOs to ensure their ability to: launch sustained policy and advocacy initiatives, ensure their operational resilience, and advance the self-reliance of refugees and host communities.

This is evidenced by 4 instances where RLOs contributed to the design of policies (Output P.1.1.1 RLOs contribute to the design and publication of at least 16 policies by the end of the program)
· In Kenya, we facilitated two RLO partners’ attendance at the August 2025 Devolution Conference, organized by Council of Governors in Kenya. As a result of their engagement, they were invited to contribute to a consultation led by the Government of Kenya’s Department of Refugee Services (DRS) and submitted a RLO Refugee Leaders’ Memorandum that steers the government’s engagement with RLOs.
· We also facilitated Uganda- and Kenya-based RLO partners’ attendance at the IGAD Thematic Roundtable on Protection and Solutions for Forcibly Displaced Populations, from 16-18 September in Nairobi. The roundtable assessed progress on implementing the IGAD Policy Framework on Refugee Protection across the IGAD Member States to develop actionable recommendations for future refugee policies in the region. According to our partners, key messages they raised during the roundtable on access to asylum, meaningful refugee participation, and partnerships were integrated into the final recommendations released by IGAD following the event. These recommendations will help to inform the design of refugee policies in IGAD Member States in the future.
· In Uganda, we supported two RLO partners to participate in a consultation convened by the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) on 17 September in Kampala to inform the draft National Refugee Policy. While Uganda is widely recognized for its progressive refugee approach, it has historically lacked a formal written policy to anchor its framework for refugee protection. The initial draft policy placed significant emphasis on refugees living in settlements. During the consultation, our partners advocated for the inclusion of refugees residing in urban areas, particularly in light of the growing number relocating from settlements to cities due to declining humanitarian assistance. As a result, the revised draft National Refugee Policy now places greater emphasis on urban refugees.
· In Ethiopia, we partnered with one RLO to encourage the Government of Ethiopia to adopt policies limiting the issuance of hand-written Conventional Travel Documents (CTDs) and transitioning toward machine-readable CTDs for refugees. Despite regional commitments across East Africa to promote refugees’ freedom of movement, the continued use of hand-written CTDs—often not recognized by other states—has undermined this right in practice. In collaboration with the RLO, we carried out a series of advocacy activities between October and December aimed at promoting the adoption of machine-readable CTDs. These efforts contributed to the adoption of a bill in February 2026 (Immigration and Citizenship Service Fee Regulation No. 587/2026), which includes provisions to enable access to machine-readable CTDs for refugees (See also Annex 6).

comment.narrative: TRUE or FALSE (1 or 0), based on evidence from discussions with RLOs of improvement of the protection of local displaced communities at the end of the project. (qualitative indicator)

TRUE
Our project contributed to improved access to protection services for refugees. Of the 6 sub-grants we disbursed to RLO partners in 2025, 5 partners implemented activities that strengthened access to protection (Output P1.2.1), exceeding our target of supporting 3 RLOs. In Kenya, one partner supported 20 refugee-led initiatives in Kakuma to formally register, helping expand the programmatic impact of RLOs in Kakuma. In Türkiye, our partners used sub-grants to sustain case management work and legal hotlines for refugees during a period where both were experiencing financial crises due to international funding cuts. One partner also conducted a legal rights awareness training targeting refugees in Trabzon in December 2025, reaching 170 refugees in the region. All the organizations that received sub-grant funding from ID in 2025 emphasized the important role that the funding had in covering their institutional costs that allow them to maintain existing activities. This was particularly important for one partner in Turkiye, who was left as the only operational NGO case management provider in Trabzon and neighboring provinces when, as a result of international funding cuts, major national NGO responders closed their operations in the Black Sea region.
Beyond support provided through sub-grants, activities conducted by ID also meaningfully contributed to improved access to protection. In September 2025, ID conducted Skill Up workshops with partners on rights and policy frameworks governing refugees – first at the global level through a virtual workshop reaching 91 refugee and host community leaders, followed by engagements at the regional level on the margins of two regional roundtables in East Africa and MENA. These workshops helped to improve our partners’ awareness of existing protection frameworks for refugees and helped to enhance our partners’ positioning on strengthening protection mechanisms for RLO operations. These trainings also complemented the skills of our partners’ staff to directly provide protection services to refugees.

3 partners helped improve access to job opportunities and development through activities in 2025 (Output P3.1.1). In Kenya, one partner trained 20 vulnerable refugee women living below the poverty line in Kakuma in a 12-week program on business development. At the conclusion of the training program, each woman received KES 30,000 in seed capital to launch or scale their own micro-enterprises. The partner also expanded access to digital livelihoods through entrepreneurship bootcamps and Freelancer Upskilling Workshops, reaching 20 digital freelancers in Kakuma. In Türkiye, one partner used its sub-grant disbursement to cover gaps in its overhead and institutional costs that sustain its advocacy operations. As a result, the partner continued to scale up its policy and advocacy targeting the Government of Türkiye to expand access to work permits for Syrian refugees registered under the Temporary Protection Status (TPS). The partner capitalized on previous policy wins to ease access to work permits for TPS-registered Syrians in Türkiye and targeted its advocacy on influencing private sector actors to formally employ Syrian refugees.

Indicator reflected in ID organizational logframe as: - Outcome P2.1 Access to education and training for local displaced communities has been maintained (if already active prior to the project) or improved; AND - Outcome P4.1 Access to improved services, facilities and information systems has increased for local displaced communities.

TRUE
Our project improved access to education and training for refugees and host communities. In 2025, 4 partners used ID sub-grants to strengthen education services in their communities (Output P2.1.1). In Türkiye, for example, one partner organized two workshops in November focused on children’s rights and 21st-century skills, reaching 30 children and 21 youth. In Uganda, another partner provided funding to one of its member organizations to facilitate access to early childhood education, aligned with national education standards, for 41 children. We also provided small stipends to 8 partner organizations, to support the participation of staff and refugee leaders in Skill Up trainings delivered under our capacity strengthening work. These trainings complemented partners’ education and training activities by equipping them with materials to replicate practical training with a wider network of refugee leaders and RLOs. In Uganda, for example, two partners used funding from their sub-grant allocation and stipend toward conducting trainings on diplomacy and advocacy with RLO leaders using materials shared by ID, cumulatively reaching 573 individuals (303 men and 270 women). These included trainings targeted at newly elected representatives of the Refugee Welfare Council (RWC). We anticipate that the number of people we reach through such trainings will increase between 2026-2028, as we begin implementing the second phase of our Skill Up training program.
Our partners also contributed to improving access to services, facilities, and information systems for refugees and host communities. 3 of the 6 partners receiving sub-grants implemented activities that improved access to critical infrastructure and social protection services using sub-grant disbursements from ID (Output P4.1.1). In Kenya, one partner allocated a part of their sub-grant disbursement toward drilling a borehole within its compound in the Kakuma Refugee Camp. Today, the borehole supports more than 500 surrounding households with access to safe drinking water during periods of water shortages. The borehole also supports access to safe drinking water for 200 refugees and staff who access the partner’s digital training center daily, helping it to also contribute towards strengthening access to digital livelihoods.

title.narrative: 2.2 % of direct funding to in-country partners which classifies as c. multi-annual funding

description.narrative:
The percentages reflect the distribution of funds to in-country partners under each category, and the sum of these percentages may not necessarily equal 100%.
ICR/overhead (indirect cost recovery): funding to support operational activities but cannot be directly allocated to activities funded by MFA. These funds support essential operational and administrative costs linked to programming capacity. Project funding: funding that is used for direct and indirect project costs Multi-annual funding: funding with a duration of 24 months or more based on the start and end dates of the original formal funding agreement (Grand Bargain) Core Capacity funding: Flexible capacity building funds transferred to the partner organisation to support their core capacity needs outlined in Indicator 1.1, but which may also be used to address other organisational capacity needs as identified by the partner. These funds need to be clearly identifiable and explained in ICP budgets. External donors: Any external funds transferred to in-country partners outside the MFA. It could include contributions from internal budgets of support partners or other institutional donors.

comment.narrative: ID did not provide direct funding to in-country partners before 2025, making the baseline 0 for this indicator.
There is no pre-defined target for this indicator, making the target "N/A".

Limited quantitative data was provided by partners regarding the distribution of funding across these categories, which constrains our ability to draw comprehensive conclusions across the full partner cohort. Only two partners provided numerical estimates of how funding is distributed. In analyzing the self-assessment survey results, it is important to reiterate that we provided annual sub-grants to 6 RLO partners, as well as Skill Up stipends to 8 partners in 2025, which formed the primary modality for funding disbursement under this project (see also Intervention Objective 3: Direct Funding).
Among the responses received, one partner reported that overhead or indirect cost recovery (ICR) funding represents approximately 13% of the total funding received from ID. This allocation reflects the portion of funding dedicated to covering organizational operating costs that cannot be directly attributed to specific programme activities but are nonetheless essential to maintaining operational capacity. Another partner reported that approximately 90–95% of the funding received from ID functions as core capacity funding, indicating a highly flexible funding structure designed to strengthen institutional capacity alongside programme implementation. The responses received on project funding or external donor contributions remain insufficient for drawing wider conclusions.
However, the limited and uneven nature of responses points to broader challenges in how this information was captured, especially when partner-reported perceptions of funding structures do not fully align with our own internal financial data. The survey relied on multiple terms, such as overhead costs, project funding, and core capacity funding, which may not have been clearly or consistently understood by partners despite efforts to provide definitions in the self-assessment survey. In addition, the use of technical or jargon-heavy language in this section may have reduced our partners’ engagement in this section of the survey, with several partners partially completing or skipping these questions altogether. This experience suggests a need to both simplify (i) how funding categories are presented, and (ii) strengthen our shared understanding with partners on funding modalities.

title.narrative: 3.1 # of in-country partners self-reporting improved participation in programming and policy-making at local, national, regional and/or global levels

description.narrative: This indicator assesses the progress of in-country partners across the following three levels: 1- Participation in Coordination Mechanism 2- Ability to influence policies and programming 3- Ability to bring the voices of affected population into responses

comment.narrative: 80% of total in-country partners

The self-assessment survey results indicate overall progress in strengthening our partners’ participation and influence, although structural barriers within the humanitarian system remain significant. At baseline, our partners reported having a small degree of access to coordination mechanisms and limited structural influence over policy processes and programming. Survey findings demonstrate that approximately 74% of our partners experienced improvement in meaningful participation across the three aggregated assessed dimensions including participation in coordination mechanisms, ability to influence policy and programming processes and the capacity to bring the voices of affected populations. These results suggest that the support provided through the project contributed to strengthening our partners’ ability to engage more actively and strategically within humanitarian and policy spaces.
At the same time, partners emphasized that meaningful participation continues to be defined by structural dynamics within the humanitarian system. While RLOs increasingly contribute to discussions and consultations, their influence over decision-making often remains limited by institutional hierarchies, access to decision-making spaces, and the structure of programme design processes.

title.narrative: 1.1 # of in-country partners self-reporting increased capacity of their self-identified objectives across at least three key areas (incl but not limited to programming, policy, fundraising, financial, administrative, human resources, fiduciary, and Strategic organizational leadership)

description.narrative: This indicator measures the number of in-country partners that report improvement in at least three areas over the program period. Key areas are defined as follows: Programming: Programming refers to the strategic design, planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of projects and activities that address the needs of affected populations and contribute to the organization’s mission. Examples of programming subcategories including but not limited to planning, programming and MEAL related to MFA's thematic objectives of the framework Migration and Displacement; and Support for Regional Refugee Responses/Opvang in de Regio (OidR) including cross cutting themes (e.g., gender, environment, and GESI) , and area related internal organizational policy development. Policy (influencing/analysis/ formulation): capacity strengthening of External policy analysis, external lobby and external advocacy capacities, and area related external policy development. (Internal policy developments do not fall under this category, for example, HR, MEAL, Procurement, etc.) Fundraising: The process of securing financial resources from diverse funding streams (e.g., donors, grants, individual contributions) to sustain operations and achieve programmatic goals. Examples of Fundraising subcategories including but not limited to identifying funding opportunities, donor engagement, and mobilizing unrestricted funding to support core organizational functions, and area related internal organizational policy development. Financial: Means the planning, management, and reporting of the organization’s financial resources to ensure transparency, sustainability, and accountability. Examples of Financial subcategories including but not limited to budgeting, financial reporting, cash flow management, financial diversification, revenue-generating activities, and non-donor funding sources, and area related internal organizational policy development. Administrative: The systems and processes that support day-to-day operational efficiency, such as procurement, logistics, and office management. examples of administrative subcategories including but not limited to office management, documentation, procurement, and compliance with policies, archiving, technological automations etc, and area related internal organizational policy development. Human resources: The function responsible for managing an organization’s workforce. HR is involved in but not limited to recruitment, employee development, performance management, compliance with labor laws, and area related internal organizational policy development. Fiduciary: refers to the ethical and legal obligation to manage organizational assets (including donor funds) responsibly, ensuring accountability and minimizing risk. Examples of subcategories including but not limited to compliance , audit, and area related internal organizational policy development. Strategic organizational leadership: Strategic planning/Leadership, decision making, Communication and visibility, networking and partnerships.

comment.narrative: At the baseline, our partners indicated the reactive and ad hoc nature of their programming, policy engagement, fundraising, human resources, and strategic leadership capacities, resulting in limited ability to engage in long-term planning. In 2025, 6 out of 9 in-country partners (67%) reported increased capacity across at least three key priority areas, meeting the requirements of Indicator 1.1. These improvements were measured through partner self-assessment surveys, where partners identified priority areas for organizational strengthening—such as programming, policy engagement, fundraising, human resources, and strategic leadership—and reported whether their capacity had improved in each area (“Yes” or “Partly”). In a small number of cases where partners did not complete all closed-response questions, qualitative evidence from narrative responses was used to validate and complement reported improvements, ensuring results were not underestimated. These findings demonstrate substantial progress toward strengthening the institutional capacity of refugee-led and local partner organizations, a core objective of the project.

title.narrative: 2.1 # of in-country partners self-reporting increased quality of funding (5- Availability of multi-year financing for preparedness, stability and quality (Quantitative, Target 100%))

description.narrative:
This indicator will measure the increased quality of funding received by in-country partners from supporting partners. - The numerical value for this indicator is measured only from the ICR/overhead and availability of multi-year financing provision to In-country partners. See below number (2 and 5). - Baseline for this indicator can be calculated only if support partners have a previous partnership with the current in-country partners. If no previous partnership then the baseline will be Zero. - Progress for this indicator is measured only within this grant framework, not related to other external donors. - The qualitative data will be assessed using the following quality of funding criteria.
Quality of funding is: 1- Funding for operating costs including relevant core capacity costs (Qualitative Description, for this criteria it still needed to have the numerical value) 2- ICR/overhead are an integral part of the funding provided to ICPs by SP with no reporting. (Quantitative, Target 100%) 3- Transparency of financial transactions and budgets (that relate to ICP's budgets,). (Qualitative Description) 4- Flexibility for ICP to make reasonable adjustments during implementation (Qualitative Description) 5- Availability of multi-year financing for preparedness, stability and quality (Quantitative, Target 100%) 6- Support actively seek to strengthen the financial sustainability of ICP (Qualitative Description) 7 - Funding is provided that is adequate to deliver a response that meets quality standards and commitments

comment.narrative:
This indicator assesses improvements in the quality of funding provided to partners by the Support Partner (SP), focusing on two key elements: (i) access to unrestricted overhead/indirect cost recovery (ICR) funding, and (ii) access to multi-year funding arrangements. Overall, survey findings suggest that the funding provided through the project incorporates several elements associated with quality funding, including overhead support for some partners, transparent financial communication, and flexibility during implementation. As ID had no prior funding relationships with partners under this project, the baseline for this indicator was zero. In 2025, 3 out of 4 responding partners (75%) reported receiving overhead or ICR funding, representing a meaningful improvement in funding quality. This type of support is critical, as it enables partners to cover core institutional costs—such as staffing, operations, and administrative functions—that are essential for organizational sustainability but are often excluded from project-based funding.
At the same time, the absence of multi-year funding arrangements within the current grant framework limits the extent to which the indicator can fully capture the improvements achieved in funding quality. No partners (0%) reported receiving multi-year funding during the reporting period. This reflects the design of our sub-granting approach in Year 2, where funding was intentionally structured as one-year grants while partnerships were being established. While multi-year funding is an important component of quality funding due to the predictability and stability it provides, it was not included at this stage of the programme. To address this gap, ID is actively exploring the introduction of multi-year funding agreements in future phases of the project (see also Section 7: Recommendations). This is expected to enhance funding predictability, strengthen partners’ financial resilience, and further improve the overall quality of funding provided.

description.narrative:
This indicator will measure the increased quality of funding received by in-country partners from supporting partners. - The numerical value for this indicator is measured only from the ICR/overhead and availability of multi-year financing provision to In-country partners. comment.narrative:
This indicator assesses improvements in the quality of funding provided to partners by the Support Partner (SP), focusing on two key elements: (i) access to unrestricted overhead/indirect cost recovery (ICR) funding, and (ii) access to multi-year funding arrangements. Overall, survey findings suggest that the funding provided through the project incorporates several elements associated with quality funding, including overhead support for some partners, transparent financial communication, and flexibility during implementation. As ID had no prior funding relationships with partners under this project, the baseline for this indicator was zero. In 2025, 3 out of 4 responding partners (75%) reported receiving overhead or ICR funding, representing a meaningful improvement in funding quality. This type of support is critical, as it enables partners to cover core institutional costs—such as staffing, operations, and administrative functions—that are essential for organizational sustainability but are often excluded from project-based funding.
At the same time, the absence of multi-year funding arrangements within the current grant framework limits the extent to which the indicator can fully capture the improvements achieved in funding quality. No partners (0%) reported receiving multi-year funding during the reporting period. This reflects the design of our sub-granting approach in Year 2, where funding was intentionally structured as one-year grants while partnerships were being established. While multi-year funding is an important component of quality funding due to the predictability and stability it provides, it was not included at this stage of the programme. To address this gap, ID is actively exploring the introduction of multi-year funding agreements in future phases of the project (see also Section 7: Recommendations). This is expected to enhance funding predictability, strengthen partners’ financial resilience, and further improve the overall quality of funding provided.
While the indicator target has therefore not yet been met due to not having rolled out multi-year funding agreements with partners in 2025, qualitative responses from partners indicate that the partnership nonetheless demonstrates several characteristics of quality funding that contribute positively to programme implementation and organizational development. The ongoing discussions around the introduction of multi-year funding arrangements suggest that further progress will be achieved during the remainder of the programme.
